title: Half-Indian Footballer Wins Racism Tribunal, Seeks £12M From Crawley Town
excerpt: Amrit Bansal-McNulty was called a "curry muncher" by manager John Yems, whose three-year FA ban was the longest ever for discrimination
body:
**A landmark ruling against racism in English football** has handed half-Indian midfielder Amrit Bansal-McNulty a partial victory in his employment tribunal case against former Crawley Town manager John Yems and Queens Park Rangers.

The London Central Employment Tribunal, presided over by Judge Nicolle, upheld three claims of racial harassment against Yems, finding that Crawley Town was vicariously liable for the manager's conduct during his tenure from 2019 to 2022. Yems subjected Bansal-McNulty to repeated racist abuse, including calling him a "curry muncher," in what the tribunal described as a pattern of discriminatory behaviour.

**Career-ending consequences and a record claim** now define the case's next chapter. Bansal-McNulty is pursuing £12 million in compensation, arguing that the sustained racial abuse caused psychological harm so severe it ended his professional football career. Yems had already received the longest discrimination ban in Football Association history — three years — after an earlier FA investigation.

**The tribunal dismissed QPR's separate claims** against Crawley Town, narrowing the liability but keeping the spotlight on how English football clubs handle racism complaints internally. The case has reignited debate about institutional accountability in the sport, particularly as UK police separately investigate racist abuse targeting four Premier League players this week.

Bansal-McNulty's case resonates with the 1.8 million-strong British Indian community that has long faced the "curry" slur as a marker of casual racism — and now has a legal precedent that such abuse in the workplace carries real consequences.
nri_angle: The case sets a legal precedent for South Asians facing racial abuse in Western workplaces, and the specific slurs used echo discrimination many Indian-Americans encounter.
author: Diaspora Desk
